items.value: Environmental change (climate change) drives resource scarcity, which in turn produces political conflict
items.reasoning: The passage sets out a chain: climate change hastens the reduction of resources, and competition over those diminishing resources then takes the form of political or even violent conflict. That is exactly what C states. A inverts the chain and adds 'always', which the passage never claims; the passage says the opposite direction, that political-looking conflicts are often resource conflicts underneath. B is not discussed at all — the passage nowhere rules out political solutions. D says identity- or ideology-based conflict 'cannot be resolved', whereas the passage only says resource conflicts are cloaked in identity or ideology, which is a claim about disguise, not about resolvability.

items.value: One should consult wisely first and then resolve firmly (and execute with perseverance)
items.reasoning: The passage's closing sentence is nearly verbatim option A: 'It is only the man who first consults wisely, then resolves firmly and then executes his purpose with inflexible perseverance ... that can advance to eminence.' B is the opposite of 'consults wisely' — the passage condemns the man who fluctuates, not the man who listens. C is not the theme; broad-mindedness is never mentioned. D captures firmness and achievement but drops the 'consult wisely' half, which the passage places first and treats as the precondition, so it is a partial reading of the same sentence.

items.value: Climate change threatens the survival of polar bears
items.reasoning: The passage records earlier and faster melting, a 30 per cent decline in summer ice, and states that the lengthening melt 'threatens to undermine the whole Arctic food web, atop which stand polar bears'. The crucial message is therefore the threat to polar bears' survival. A misreports the facts — the passage says the summer melt period is lengthening, not that summer is short, and says nothing about temperature figures. B is invented; relocation to the South Pole is nowhere in the text. C reverses the causal direction: the passage says the collapse of the food web endangers the bears at its top, not that the food chains depend on the bears.

items.value: Open defecation will end only when people stop perceiving toilet use and pit-emptying as polluting
items.reasoning: The passage names two critical elements — ideas of purity and pollution, and unwillingness to have pits or septic tanks fill because they must be emptied — and insists that to eradicate open defecation 'they have to be confronted and dealt properly'. Changing that perception is precisely B. A says these ideas cannot be removed, which contradicts the passage's call to confront and deal with them. C is a broader fatalism the passage does not endorse. D introduces civic sense and privacy, neither of which the passage mentions.

items.value: Growth measured by GDP alone is neither desirable nor sustainable
items.reasoning: The passage contrasts a 50 per cent rise in GDP with a mere 6 per cent rise in inclusive wealth, and states that GDP-driven performance 'has only harmed' human capital (up just 8 per cent) and natural capital (down 30 per cent). The inference is that GDP-only growth damages the underlying wealth base and so cannot be sustained — option B. A is a policy prescription about one component and misses the passage's central contrast between GDP and inclusive wealth. C is vague and not what the figures show; GDP performance was in fact strong. D again picks one component, and the passage notes human capital did grow, just slowly.

items.value: Labour reforms are needed so that India's large labour force is used productively
items.reasoning: The passage explicitly frames labour reforms as 'the way to unlock double-digit growth', then supplies the evidence of a labour force that is 93 per cent unorganized, employment CAGR down to 0.5 per cent, and 14 million jobs created against a labour-force increase of about 15 million. The rational inference is that reform is required to absorb and use that force productively. C is refuted by the same figures: with jobs lagging the labour force, double-digit growth is not imminent. D overreaches — the passage says India's youth surplus 'could fill the gap', but never says the surplus is skilled, and 93 per cent unorganized suggests otherwise. A imports population control, which the passage never raises; the youth surplus is presented as an opportunity, not a problem.

items.value: Work is an inescapable obligation for human beings; only the amount of leisure is negotiable
items.reasoning: Three of the passage's four sentences argue that work is compulsory: freedom from the obligation to work is 'unnatural' and 'ought to be illegal', nature ordains famine if the race stops working, and 'we cannot escape from this tyranny'. That makes A the main idea. C fastens on the single word 'tyranny' while ignoring that the author treats work as a natural and just obligation rather than an imposition to be endured. D is not argued at all. RUNNER-UP: B ('a balance between work and leisure'), which would win if the closing sentence — 'The question we have to settle is how much leisure we can afford to allow ourselves' — were read as the culminating point rather than a subordinate corollary; on that reading the passage is about apportioning work and leisure. I set it aside because the passage concedes no choice about working at all, and only the residual quantity of leisure is left open, which is a weaker claim than 'balance'.

items.value: Habits make living easier by simplifying life and sparing us fresh thought about routine things
items.reasoning: The passage says outright that habits 'simplify the mechanism of life', that 'we could not get on without them', and that without them existence would be 'an impossible confusion' — all of which say habits make it easier for us to live. A is the reverse of the author's view. B is not claimed; nothing suggests habits make us more precise, only more automatic. D is the trap: 'mechanize' picks up the word 'mechanism' and the idea of acting automatically, but the author's point is that habits simplify the mechanism of life to our benefit, whereas 'mechanize our lives' carries a criticism the passage never makes.

items.value: At least one party-Y supporter is a friend of some party-X supporter (friendship being mutual)
items.reasoning: Let S be the set of party-X supporters who both knew Z and supported his campaign strategy. The clause 'but some of them had friends in party Y' asserts that S is non-empty and that at least one member of S has a friend who belongs to party Y. Friendship is mutual, so that party-Y person is likewise a friend of a party-X supporter — which is exactly B, and it must be true. C and D are contradicted by the very existence of S: some party-X supporters did know Z and did support his strategy. A concerns what party-Y supporters agreed to, on which the statement says nothing — it only tells us what members of S did not agree to.

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 are the ones that do not follow; statement 1 does follow
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: 'some of them had friends in party Y' guarantees that the set of party-X supporters who knew Z (and backed his strategy) is non-empty, so some party-X supporters certainly knew Z. Statement 2 is not correct: the given information says nothing whatever about party-X supporters who opposed Z's strategy, so their knowing Z cannot be concluded. Statement 3 is not correct, and is in fact false: the same existential clause shows that some party-X supporters did support Z's campaign strategy. The question asks which are NOT correct, so the answer is 2 and 3 only.

items.value: 22 working days (a 28-day February: 4 Sundays plus the 2nd and 4th Saturdays = 6 holidays)
items.reasoning: Every month contains at least four Saturdays, so the 2nd and 4th Saturdays are always exactly 2 holidays, and Saturdays never coincide with Sundays. A 28-day February is exactly four weeks and therefore has exactly 4 Sundays whatever day it begins on, giving 4 + 2 = 6 holidays and 28 - 6 = 22 working days. No month can do better: a 29-day February can reach at most 5 Sundays, giving 29 - 7 = 22 again; a 30-day month gives at most 30 - 7 = 23 and a 31-day month at most 31 - 7 = 24. An exhaustive check over a century of calendars confirms 22 as the minimum.

items.value: 64/729 of the population is left after six years
items.reasoning: If one-third migrates each year, two-thirds of the community remains at the end of each year, and with no other growth the fraction remaining compounds. After six years the leftover is (2/3)^6 = 2^6/3^6 = 64/729. Option C (32/729) corresponds to (2/3)^5 x (1/2), and options A and B use 243 = 3^5, i.e. five years' worth of denominator, so all three are off by one year or one factor of two.

items.value: Mathematics is the last test; the order is Physics, Biology, Chemistry, Mathematics
items.reasoning: 'Chemistry is conducted exactly after two tests are held' fixes Chemistry on day 3. 'The Physics test is held before the test which is conducted after Biology' requires that a test follow Biology, so Biology cannot be on day 4, and Physics must fall before that following test. Biology on day 1 would force Physics before day 2, i.e. on day 1, which is already Biology's — impossible. So Biology is on day 2, the test after it is Chemistry on day 3, and Physics must precede day 3 without clashing with Biology, putting Physics on day 1. Mathematics takes the only day left, day 4. Enumerating all 24 orderings yields this single arrangement.

items.value: B has the highest income; the ordering is B > A = C > D
items.reasoning: From 'A earns half as much as the sum of the income of B and D', B + D = 2A. Substituting into A + C = B + D gives A + C = 2A, so C = A. Putting C = A into A + B > C + D gives A + B > A + D, hence B > D. Since B + D = 2A with B > D, B must exceed the average A, so B > A. Combining, B > A = C > D, and B's income is the highest.

items.value: Only conclusion I follows — a natural gift such as a good voice still needs nurturing through practice
items.reasoning: The statement says a good voice is a natural gift but that one must keep practising to improve and excel, which is precisely the claim that natural gifts need nurturing and care, so conclusion I follows. Conclusion II does not: the statement speaks only about someone who has the natural gift and says nothing about a person whose voice is not good, so nothing about that case can be drawn from it. C requires the two conclusions to be mutually exclusive alternatives, which they are not, and D is ruled out because I does follow.

items.value: The shortest pillar is Y at 163 cm (X = 201 cm, Z = 182 cm)
items.reasoning: In each chance a spider makes a net gain equal to climb minus slip, except on the final chance, when it reaches the top and does not slip back. A gains 5 cm per chance, so X = 39x5 + 6 = 201 cm. B gains 4 cm per chance, so Y = 39x4 + 7 = 163 cm. C gains 4.5 cm per chance, so Z = 39x4.5 + 6.5 = 182 cm. The shortest is 163 cm. The reading is confirmed by the option list itself: this method yields 163 and 182, both of which are printed as options, whereas counting a slip on the final chance too would give 160, 200 and 180, none of which appears.

items.value: Rights aim at both individual and social good
items.reasoning: The quoted definition ties the two together explicitly: rights are conditions of SOCIAL well-being that are indispensable to the true development of the CITIZEN. The social conditions are the means and the individual's development is the end, so neither element can be dropped. A and B each keep only one half of the definition, and D directly contradicts it by severing individual good from social well-being, which the sentence presents as inseparable.

items.value: 16th from the bottom (the merit list has 37 names)
items.reasoning: The failed students' names are removed before the merit list is drawn up, so the list contains 52 - 15 = 37 students. If Ramesh is 22nd from the top of a list of 37, his position from the bottom is 37 - 22 + 1 = 16th. The common error is to work with the full class of 52, which would give 31st, or to forget the +1 in the position formula, which would give 15th.

items.value: Q is the father of P — P is R's son and R is Q's wife
items.reasoning: Reading the expression in pairs, P + R means P is the son of R, and R - Q means R is the wife of Q. So R is female, Q is her husband, and P is R's son; on the standard convention of these relation-coding questions Q is therefore the father of P. A is impossible because P is the son, not the parent. B is impossible because Q, being R's husband, is male and cannot be P's wife. RUNNER-UP: D, 'None of the above', which would win on a strictly literal reading, since a boy being the son of a woman and that woman being someone's wife does not by itself entail that the husband is the boy's father — Q could be a stepfather. I set that aside because these coding questions treat the spouse of a parent as the other parent, and no other option is even close; a reviewer suspecting the setter wanted the strict reading should look at D first.

items.value: Gopal gains — the phone returns to him at 99 per cent of what he originally paid for it (a 1 per cent gain on the round trip)
items.reasoning: Take Gopal's cost as 100. He sells to Ram at 110. Ram's loss of 10 per cent is on Ram's own cost of 110, so Ram sells back at 0.9 x 110 = 99. The successive multipliers are 1.1 x 0.9 = 0.99, so the phone comes back to its original owner at 1 per cent below what he first paid — a gain of 1 per cent for Gopal, and certainly not a loss, since he received 110 and paid back only 99. A is the naive answer that assumes the two 10 per cent changes cancel, which they do not because they are computed on different bases, and D halves the correct figure. RUNNER-UP: B, 'Loss 1%', which would win if the setter were applying the standard x-squared-over-100 rule in its usual form, where a 10 per cent rise followed by a 10 per cent fall is quoted as a net 1 per cent LOSS; that rule describes the fall in the price, and here the party who benefits from the lower price is Gopal, so calling it his loss inverts the direction. CAUTION - possible defect: on a full cash accounting Gopal is better off by 11, not 1 (he paid 100, received 110 and paid 99, ending with the phone and a net outlay of 89, i.e. an 11 per cent gain), and no option offers 11 per cent, so the option set only supports the looser price-multiplier reading.
